A drawing is a record of what we notice. One drawing can show where a patch of sunlight falls. It cannot show whether the patch changes position. In this booklet, we will watch the sunlight on our classroom floor and make drawings we can compare.

We will observe over three school days. Work with the same partner each day. Look at the beginning of the morning lesson and immediately after lunch. That gives you six observation spaces. Your drawings will record the position of the light you can see. They will not answer every question about why it is there.

Mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan. Write the time beside it. If part of the edge is fuzzy, mark that part with a dotted line. You have a pencil and a ruler. A ruler can help you draw a straight line. It cannot make a fuzzy edge sharp. If two groups draw the edge differently, compare what each group noticed before deciding whether either drawing needs to change.

Sometimes there may be no patch to see. Write “no patch visible” in the space for that observation and leave its floor plan unmarked. Yesterday’s patch belongs in yesterday’s drawing. Recording that no patch is visible counts as an observation. It does not give you a measurement of the patch’s position. The curtains will stay in their usual position. We will not control the clouds or record how thick they are.

At the end, compare all six observation spaces with your partner. Write one sentence about a pattern your observations support and one question that remains. If too few patches were visible to establish a pattern, say so. Explain which observations are missing.

There is no particular pattern you must discover. Your booklet needs to show what you could see and what you could not. A careful record of a patch nobody could see can be more useful than a confident drawing of where someone thinks it was.

# Watching the Light

A drawing is a choice about what to notice. In this booklet we will notice one thing: where a patch of sunlight falls on the classroom floor.

## What we will do

The activity takes place over three school days. You will work with the same partner each day. You will make an observation at the beginning of the morning lesson and another immediately after lunch. That gives six observations in all.

We do this more than once because one drawing cannot show whether a position changes. It shows only where the light was, once. Several drawings can show more.

Our drawings will show where the light can be seen. They will not tell us why it is there. That is a different question, and the drawings do not answer it.

## How to mark the floor plan

Mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan. Write the time beside it.

Sometimes the edge of the light is fuzzy. Where it is, draw that part with a dotted line. Do not decide that the edge must be sharp just because a sharp line is easier to draw. A pencil and ruler are provided, but the ruler does not make a fuzzy edge less fuzzy. It is good for straight lines. It cannot tell you where the light ends.

You may find that another group has marked the edge differently. Do not change your drawing straight away, and do not tell them to change theirs. First compare what each of you noticed. Then decide whether either drawing needs to change.

## When there is no light

Some days the patch may not be visible. When that happens, write "no patch visible" in the space for that observation. Leave the map unmarked. Do not draw where the patch was yesterday. That would be a map of yesterday.

"No patch visible" counts as an observation. It does not count as a measurement of the patch's position, because there was no position to measure.

The curtains will stay in their usual position. We will not control the clouds, and we will not record how thick they are. So we will not know why a patch is missing. We will know only that we did not see it.

## At the end

Compare all six observation spaces with your partner. Then write:

- one sentence about a pattern you can support
- one question that remains

Perhaps too few patches were visible to show a pattern. If so, say that, and explain which observations are missing.

You are not required to discover a particular pattern. A careful account of what could not be observed can be more useful than a confident account of a patch nobody saw.

Welcome to the garden! Your assigned bed has the same number as your membership card. Some painted numbers have faded, so check the plan on the noticeboard if you are unsure. Please ask a steward before planting in a bed whose number you cannot read. The narrow strip beside the compost bins is planted collectively; it is not an unclaimed bed.

Tools with blue handles are shared. Please return them to the shed before you leave, even if you plan to come back later that evening. Tools without blue handles may belong to another gardener, so do not assume they are shared. You will find the shed code on your membership card. The watering rota covers the collective strip and the young fruit trees, but not individual beds—even those belonging to gardeners on the rota. If you will be away, you can arrange separately for another gardener to water your bed. Only add the arrangement to the noticeboard once they have agreed, so a request does not look like a job someone has accepted.

Weeds without seed heads can go into the green compost bay. Put weeds with seed heads into the covered brown bin. Welcome to the garden! We're glad you're here. This note covers the basics, and the stewards are always happy to help with anything it doesn't answer.

**Your bed**
Your assigned bed is marked with the number on your membership card. Some of the painted numbers have faded, so if you're unsure, check the plan on the noticeboard. That's the reliable guide. If you still can't read a bed's number, please ask a steward before planting in it. One thing to know: the narrow strip beside the compost bins isn't an unclaimed bed. It's planted collectively by all of us.

**Shared tools and the shed**
Tools with a blue handle belong to the shared collection. Please return them to the shed before you leave, even if you plan to come back later that evening. Tools without a blue handle may belong to another gardener, so don't assume they're shared. The shed code is on your membership card. When you leave, close the door behind you, because rain reaches the lower shelves when it's left open.

**Watering**
The watering rota covers the collective strip and the young fruit trees. It doesn't cover individual beds, including the beds of people who are on the rota. If you'll be away, you're welcome to arrange for another gardener to water your bed. Only add that arrangement to the noticeboard once they've agreed, so a request isn't mistaken for a job someone has accepted.

**Weeds and compost**
Weeds without seed heads can go in the green compost bay. Weeds with seed heads go in the covered brown bin. If you can't tell whether a plant has set seed, put it in the brown bin and ask at the next steward session. That's just a sorting precaution, not a judgment on anyone's gardening.

**Getting help**
Stewards are usually around on Saturday mornings, and the noticeboard lists the next session and any cancellations. Please don't hesitate to ask. We'd much rather answer a small question before you plant than help move a thriving crop out of someone else's bed.

We compared two worksheets for subtracting background from fluorescence measurements. The current worksheet requires an operator to enter a blank reading separately for each sample; the proposed worksheet imports the blank reading from the instrument log to reduce transcription. The comparison assessed agreement between corrected values and the time required to produce them. It did not assess accuracy relative to a known true concentration, and no certified reference material was included.

Twenty-four aliquots from eight prepared solutions, with three aliquots per solution, were measured in one session in a fixed order by solution number. Both worksheets processed the same instrument readings; each aliquot was measured only once. The operator completed the manual worksheet before the imported worksheet was generated and could not see the imported results during manual entry. Although each solution contributed multiple aliquots, the worksheet comparison did not include independent repeat measurements of each aliquot’s instrument signal.

In the initial comparison, corrected values agreed at the instrument’s displayed precision for 21 of the 24 aliquots. All three differences occurred in the final solution, where a single blank entry had been copied into three rows of the manual worksheet. Inspection of the saved instrument log showed that this entry was 0.2 fluorescence units higher than the blank assigned to those rows in the log, making the manual corrected values 0.2 units lower. In a separate correction performed after the initial comparison, replacing the copied entry with the logged blank brought all 24 corrected values into agreement at the displayed precision.

The initial discrepancies are consistent with a transcription error propagated across three rows, rather than three independent transcription errors. They cannot be used to estimate a routine operator error rate: only one operator participated, and that operator knew the comparison concerned data entry. Agreement after correction supports the conclusion that the import applied the intended subtraction to these inputs. It does not establish agreement beyond the displayed precision, accuracy relative to true concentration, or correct blank assignment in future instrument logs.

The imported worksheet took four minutes to produce, compared with eleven minutes for manual entry and checking—a seven-minute reduction in this session. These timings excluded instrument operation and the subsequent discrepancy investigation. The observed reduction applies to this session and its particular number of rows; whether it persists when log formats change or an operator must resolve a missing blank was not assessed.

## Background Subtraction: Manual Versus Imported Blank Values

### Purpose

In this fluorescence workflow, the current worksheet requires an operator to enter the blank reading by hand for each sample. We compared it with a proposed worksheet that imports the blank reading from the instrument log. The aim was to reduce transcription errors. Removing manual entry might also change agreement between the two methods, but this comparison measures agreement between corrected values only. It does not assess either worksheet against a known true concentration, and no certified reference material was included.

### Design

Twenty-four aliquots were prepared from eight solutions, with three aliquots per solution, and all were measured in one session. Both worksheets processed the same instrument readings. Each aliquot was measured once, so the comparison contains no independent repeats of the instrument signal, even though it contains more than one aliquot per prepared solution.

Measurement order was fixed by solution number. The manual worksheet was completed before the imported worksheet was generated, and the operator could not see the imported results while entering manual values.

One blank entry had been copied into three rows of the manual worksheet. The saved instrument log showed that the copied entry was 0.2 fluorescence units higher than the blank assigned to those rows. The manual corrected values were therefore 0.2 units lower than the imported values.

### Correction

After the initial comparison, the copied entry was replaced with the logged blank. With this change, the corrected values agreed for all 24 aliquots at displayed precision. This correction was made after the initial comparison and is reported separately from it. The 24-of-24 agreement therefore describes the corrected manual worksheet, not the original entries.

### Interpretation

The initial differences are consistent with a transcription mechanism in this session. They should not be read as an estimate of a routine operator error rate. Only one operator used the worksheet, and that operator knew the comparison concerned data entry. The three affected aliquots also do not represent three independent transcription errors, because they trace to a single copied entry.

The absence of displayed differences after correction is useful evidence that the import applied the intended subtraction to these inputs. It does not establish agreement at greater precision, and it does not show that blank assignment will be correct in future instrument logs.

### Timing

The imported worksheet took four minutes to produce, and manual entry and checking took eleven minutes. These times exclude instrument operation and the later investigation of the discrepancy, and they reflect this session's number of rows. We have not measured whether the time saving persists when log formats change or when an operator must resolve a missing blank.

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might reduce the time water remained above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed during four storms before and four storms after a cover change. The three drains on the lower street received new covers; the three on the upper street retained their existing covers. Allocation was not random: crews selected the lower street because it had received more complaints.

Fixed cameras recorded the minutes water remained above a painted reference line at each drain during each storm. All 48 drain-storm observations were available. A recorded duration of zero indicates no visible water above the line, not an absence of runoff. Across the twelve observations for each street in each period, mean duration fell from 18 to 10 minutes on the lower street and from 9 to 7 minutes on the upper street. The lower street therefore showed an eight-minute reduction, compared with a two-minute reduction on the upper street. This larger reduction can inform further study, but the comparison does not by itself establish an effect of the new covers.

Several factors limit interpretation. The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier storms. Neither street had a local gauge, and within-storm rainfall intensity was not measured. Crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because the initial quantity of leaves was not recorded, cleaning cannot be assumed to explain the larger improvement on the lower street. Equally, cleaning cannot be dismissed as irrelevant simply because both streets received it. These uncertainties, together with the nonrandom allocation of covers, leave the contribution of the cover change unresolved.

The camera records establish shorter durations above the reference line at both sets of drains during the later period. They do not establish increased drainage capacity, which was not directly measured, or fewer flooded properties, which was not measured at all. The pilot included no property-damage observations. Peak water depth could also change in a way that matters even if duration remained unchanged, but peak depth was not extracted from the images.

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and debris quantities before cleaning. These measures would address some of the present ambiguities, although rotation alone would not make storms identical. The existing recordings remain useful for describing conditions during these eight storms and assessing the practicality of the camera-based duration measure. Staff reported that every recording could be scored; whether different scorers assign the same duration remains untested.

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover shortens the time water stands above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed across eight storms: four before a cover change and four after. The three drains on the lower street received new covers. The three drains on the upper street kept their existing covers. The lower street was selected because crews had received more complaints there, so cover allocation was not random.

*What was measured*

A fixed camera at each drain recorded the number of minutes water remained above a painted reference line during each storm. A recorded duration of zero means no water was visible above the line. It does not mean the drain received no runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations were available for scoring.

Mean recorded duration, in minutes, across the twelve observations per street and period:

| Street | Before change | After change |
|---|---|---|
| Lower (covers changed) | 18 | 10 |
| Upper (covers retained) | 9 | 7 |

Durations fell at both sets of drains in the later period. The fall was larger on the street where covers were changed. That difference may help in deciding what to study next, but it does not by itself identify a cover effect.

*Why the comparison does not isolate a cover effect*

Two conditions changed alongside the covers, and neither can be separated from the cover change using the pilot's records.

- **Rainfall differed between periods.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier four. No gauge was installed on either street, and no within-storm intensity measurements exist. The pilot therefore cannot say how much of the shorter durations reflects lighter rain.
- **All six drains were cleaned on the day the covers were changed.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from every drain. Because the initial quantity of leaves was not recorded, the cleaning does not automatically explain why the lower street improved more. For the same reason, it cannot be dismissed as irrelevant simply because both streets were cleaned. If the lower street had more debris to begin with, cleaning alone could account for part or all of the larger reduction there.

*What the measure does and does not capture*

The camera records show shorter durations above the reference line. This is a narrower result than it may appear.

- It is not a measurement of drainage capacity, which was not directly measured.
- It is not a measurement of fewer flooded properties, which was not measured at all. The pilot collected no property-damage observations.
- It is not a measurement of peak water depth. A change in peak depth could matter even where recorded duration did not change, but peak depth was not extracted from the images.

*What remains unresolved*

The pilot does not establish whether the new cover shortens standing-water duration. The observed reduction on the lower street is consistent with a cover effect, with the effect of cleaning, with lighter rainfall, or with some combination. The design cannot distinguish among these.

One further uncertainty concerns the measure itself. Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. The pilot has not tested whether different scorers assign the same duration to the same recording, so the reliability of the camera-based measure is unconfirmed.

*Proposed follow-up*

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains, install local rainfall gauges to record intensity on each street, and record the quantity of debris at each drain before any cleaning. Those steps would address the allocation, rainfall, and cleaning ambiguities described above. Rotation alone would not make storms identical, so rainfall measurement would still be needed to interpret differences between periods.

The existing recordings retain two uses. They describe standing-water duration at these six drains across these eight storms. They also provide material for testing whether independent scorers produce consistent durations, which would establish whether the camera-based measure is practical for future work.

## Findings

### Design and allocation

The pilot compared two streets over eight storms: four before and four after a change to a different grate cover. Covers were changed at the three drains on the lower street. The three drains on the upper street kept their original covers and served as a comparison. The lower street was selected because crews had received more complaints there, so the cover change was not randomly assigned, and the two streets may differ in ways the pilot did not measure.

### Measurement

A fixed camera recorded, for each drain during each storm, the number of minutes that water stood above a painted reference line. All 48 drain-storm observations were available. A recorded duration of zero means no visible water above that line. It does not mean the drain received no runoff. The measure therefore reflects only water above the reference line, not total inflow or drainage performance.

Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. Scoring agreement between different scorers has not been tested, so the reliability of the duration measure is not yet established.

### Observed durations

On the lower street, the mean recorded duration across the twelve observations fell from 18 minutes before the cover change to 10 minutes after it. On the upper street, the mean fell from 9 minutes to 7 minutes. The reduction was larger on the street where covers were changed.

This comparison does not isolate a cover effect. The lower street had higher durations before the change, and the two streets were not assigned comparably. The difference in reductions is a description of the recordings, not an estimate of the cover's effect.

### Factors that could explain the change

Several factors were present during the same period and cannot be separated from the cover change with the current data:

- **Rainfall.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier storms. No gauge was installed on either street, and within-storm intensity was not measured, so local rainfall differences between streets and periods are unknown.
- **Cleaning.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because all six drains were cleaned, cleaning cannot account for the difference between the streets by itself. However, the initial quantity of leaves was not recorded, so cleaning may still have interacted with the cover change in ways the pilot cannot detect.

### What was not measured

- Drainage capacity was not measured directly.
- Flooding of properties was not measured. The pilot has no property-damage observations.
- Peak water depth was not extracted from the images. A change in peak depth could matter even if recorded duration did not change, so the duration results do not establish whether depth changed.

The camera records show shorter durations above the reference line at both sets of drains in the later period. They do not establish the cause of that pattern, and they do not show any change in drainage capacity or flood outcomes.

### Unresolved questions

- Whether the cover change caused the reduction on the lower street, given non-random allocation and the differences in rainfall and cleaning.
- Whether the duration measure gives consistent results across different scorers.
- Whether changes in peak depth, drainage capacity, or flooding accompany the changes in duration.

### Proposed follow-up

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and leaf debris before cleaning. Rotation would address some of the present ambiguities, though it would not make storms identical. The existing recordings remain useful for describing these eight storms and for testing whether the camera-based duration measure can be applied in practice.

# Findings

## What was measured

The pilot asked whether a different grate cover might shorten the time water stayed above the pavement after rain. We observed six drains on two streets during eight storms: four before a cover change and four after. The three drains on the lower street received the new covers. The three on the upper street kept their original covers. Cover allocation was not random. The lower street was chosen because crews had received more complaints there.

For each drain in each storm, a fixed camera recorded the minutes that water stood above a painted reference line. A duration of zero means no visible water above that line. It does not mean the drain received no runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations (6 drains × 8 storms) were available.

| Street | Cover change | Mean minutes above line, before (12 observations) | Mean minutes above line, after (12 observations) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lower | New covers | 18 | 10 | −8 |
| Upper | Original covers | 9 | 7 | −2 |

Recorded durations were shorter at both sets of drains in the later period, and the reduction was larger on the lower street. This is a description of the recordings. It may help in deciding what to study next, but it does not by itself identify an effect of the cover.

## What the measurements cannot explain

Several factors changed or varied alongside the covers, and the pilot cannot separate them:

- **Non-random allocation.** The lower street was selected because it had more complaints, and it also started with longer durations (18 minutes against 9). The two streets may differ in ways that affect both ponding and how they change over time, so the comparison between them is not a like-for-like test.
- **Rainfall.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier four. Neither street had its own gauge, and the pilot has no within-storm intensity measurements. Lighter rain alone could produce shorter durations at both sets of drains, and we cannot say how much of the change it accounts for.
- **Simultaneous cleaning.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. The initial quantity of leaves was not recorded. We therefore cannot say that cleaning explains why the lower street improved more, and we cannot rule it out. Cleaning both streets does not make it irrelevant, because the lower street may have had more debris to remove.

## What was not measured

The camera records show shorter durations above the line. They should not be read as evidence of the following:

- **Drainage capacity.** It was not directly measured, so an increase in capacity is not established.
- **Flooded properties.** The pilot made no property-damage observations, and fewer flooded properties is not something these data can show.
- **Peak water depth.** A change in peak depth could matter even if duration did not change, but depth was not extracted from the images.

## Reliability of the duration measure

Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. We have not tested whether different scorers assign the same duration to the same recording, so the consistency of the measure is unknown.

## Possible follow-up design

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and the amount of debris before cleaning. That would address some of the ambiguities above, though rotation alone would not make storms identical. Separately, a scorer-agreement check would show whether the camera-based duration measure is dependable.

## What the existing recordings can support

The recordings remain useful for describing these eight storms and for assessing whether camera-based duration is a practical measure. They do not establish that the new covers shortened ponding.

Returning keyboard focus to a cell puts the cursor back. Does it put the user back in context? This hypothetical study asked whether speaking the current row label after a note closes helps screen-reader users return to a table.

Twelve experienced screen-reader users completed four tasks with each of two versions. One spoke the row label when the note closed. The existing version returned focus to the same cell without the added cue. Six participants used the cue version first; six used the existing version first. The two task sets used different tables, and table assignments were reversed for half of each order group.

We timed the interval from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note was outside that interval. We calculated each participant’s mean completion time for each version, then took the median of those twelve means. That median was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. The three-second gap is a difference between two medians, not the median of twelve within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower personal mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means at the recorded precision. We have not calculated a confidence interval or performed a significance test. These descriptive results do not establish a reliable speed benefit.

Did the cue help people feel oriented? Nine participants said it did in the closing interview. Four of those nine also described occasions when it interrupted speech they were still listening to. The same cue could help with orientation and interfere with listening. These reports describe participants’ experience; they are not a measured improvement in search performance.

The other three participants did not report an orientation benefit. None asked for the feature to be removed from the prototype, but that does not tell us whether they wanted it enabled by default. We did not ask participants to choose a default.

The ordering scheme reduced the alignment between version and practice without removing every possible learning effect. A search strategy learned in the first task set may have carried into the second. The study also leaves two scope questions open: how less experienced users would respond, and how the cue would work in large tables. All participants were experienced, and the prototype tables fit within one screen.

For the product team, an orientation benefit is plausible for some users under these tasks. Added speech can also compete with ongoing speech. That competition needs attention even if a time difference eventually proves reliable. A next version could make the cue interruptible, then test whether users can get the location information without losing speech they still need. We did not implement or test that behavior here. The present timings cannot serve as evidence for it.

# Spoken Location Cue After Closing a Note: Research Summary

## Question

Does a spoken cue that announces the current row label help screen-reader users return to a table after they close a note? And if it does, what does the cue cost?

## Prototype and Design

We compared two versions:

- **Cue version:** When a note closes, the current row label is spoken.
- **Existing version:** Keyboard focus returns to the same cell, with no added cue.

Twelve experienced screen-reader users each completed four tasks with each version. Six used the cue version first and six used the existing version first. The two sets of tasks used different tables. For half of each order group, the assignment of tables to versions was reversed.

We timed from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note was outside the timed interval.

## Timing Results

- Median of participant-level mean completion times: **38 seconds** with the cue, **41 seconds** without it.
- This compares two medians of participant means. It is not the median of twelve within-person differences.
- Seven participants had a lower personal mean with the cue. Three had a higher mean. Two were equal at the recorded precision.
- We have not calculated a confidence interval or run a significance test.

So the timing data points in one direction, but it does not establish a reliable difference. Seven of twelve is a split, not a pattern we can call settled.

## Orientation Feedback

In the closing interview, nine of twelve participants said the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of those nine also described moments when the cue interrupted speech they were still listening to.

The other three reported no orientation benefit. None asked for the feature to be removed from the prototype.

Two points to keep apart:

- Not asking for removal is not the same as wanting the cue on by default. Participants were not asked to choose a default, so we have no data on that.
- This is exploratory interview feedback. It is not a measured performance result.

## Limitations

- **Order effects:** Counterbalancing removed the complete alignment of version and practice, but not every learning effect. Some participants may have learned a search strategy in the first set of tasks that carried into the second.
- **Participants:** Less experienced users were not recruited. We don't know how they would respond.
- **Table size:** The tables fit on one screen in the prototype. The study says nothing about performance on large tables.

## Interpretation

The orientation benefit is plausible for some users under these tasks. The interruption reports show that added speech can compete with speech the user is already hearing. That competition is a design question regardless of whether the timing difference proves reliable.

## Next Steps

A next version could make the cue interruptible, so it yields to ongoing speech. We did not implement or test that behavior. The timings in this study should not be cited as evidence that an interruptible cue performs better.

Open questions for the next round:

- Does the timing difference hold with more participants and a confidence interval?
- How do less experienced users respond?
- Does the effect hold on tables larger than one screen?
- Do users prefer the cue on by default when asked directly?

When a screen-reader user closes a note on a table cell, our current version returns keyboard focus to that same cell. Focus is back, but does the user know where it landed? We built a version that speaks the current row label when the note closes. This study asked whether that spoken location cue helps users get back to the table.

Twelve experienced screen-reader users each completed four tasks with the cue version and four with the existing version, which returns focus without the cue. Six started with the cue version and six started with the existing version. The two sets of tasks used different tables. For half of each order group, we reversed which table went with which version.

We timed from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Time spent reading the note was not included. Each session ended with an interview.

We took each participant's mean completion time for each version. The median of those twelve means was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. That is a difference between two medians. It is not the median of each person's own difference. We have not calculated a confidence interval or run a significance test.

Looking at individuals:

- Three had a higher mean time with the cue.

Nine of the twelve said the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of those nine also described times when the cue interrupted speech they were still listening to. The other three did not report an orientation benefit, but none of them asked for the cue to be removed from the prototype.

# Spoken row cue after closing a note: research summary

## The question

Does a spoken location cue help screen-reader users return to a table after opening a note? We built a version that speaks the current row label when the note closes. The existing version returns keyboard focus to the same cell and adds no cue.

## What we did

Twelve experienced screen-reader users each completed four tasks with each version. Six started with the cue version and six with the existing version. The two sets of tasks used different tables, and for half of each order group we reversed which tables went with which version.

We timed from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note was outside that interval.

## What we found

**Time.** The median of the twelve participant-level mean completion times was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. That is a difference between two medians, not the median of twelve within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower personal mean with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two were equal at the recorded precision. We have not calculated a confidence interval or run a significance test, so we can't say whether the three-second gap is reliable.

**Interviews.** Nine participants said the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of those nine also described times when the cue cut across speech they were still listening to. The other three reported no orientation benefit. None of the twelve asked us to remove the feature.

That last point is easy to over-read. Not asking for removal is not the same as wanting the cue on by default, and we never asked participants to choose a default. The interview comments are self-reported impressions, not measured performance.

## What this supports

An orientation benefit looks plausible for some users on these tasks. The timing direction is consistent with that, but it is weak evidence on its own.

The study also shows that added speech can compete with speech the user is still hearing. That is a design problem whether or not a time difference eventually proves reliable. A faster cue that talks over the user is not an obvious win.

## What this does not support

- **Learning effects.** Our counterbalancing broke the complete alignment between version and practice, but it did not remove every possible learning effect. A search strategy picked up in the first set of tasks may have carried into the second.
- **Less experienced users.** We did not recruit them, so we don't know how they would respond.
- **Large tables.** The prototype tables were short enough to fit on one screen. We have no performance evidence for large tables, which is where a location cue might matter most.
- **Default behavior.** The data say nothing about whether the cue should ship enabled.

## What to do next

An interruptible cue is a reasonable next version. We did not implement or test it here, so the current timings are not evidence for it and should not be presented that way.

The next test should follow the user's attention, not just the clock. Does the cue arrive while the user is still listening to something else? Does the user act on it or talk past it? The same study should include less experienced users and tables longer than one screen, and should ask participants directly about defaults. If we want a claim about speed, we also need the interval estimate and test we haven't yet run.

# Diagrams Beside Questions or on a Reference Page: A Small Worksheet Comparison

*This report uses hypothetical evidence.*

## Summary

We compared two versions of a worksheet that asked pupils to explain why the same amount of water looks different in a tall vessel and a wide vessel. Version A placed a diagram beside each question. Version B placed the same diagrams together on a reference page. In this comparison, a larger share of Version A answers earned full credit. The comparison cannot show that the layout caused the difference, because pupil assignment and teacher help were not controlled.

## What Was Compared

The two versions were identical in wording, diagrams, and question order. The only difference was where the diagrams appeared. Four classes used the materials during one lesson. Two classes received Version A and two received Version B. Teachers chose the version for their classes before they saw any pupil responses.

Teachers used the same written instructions and could answer pupil questions during the lesson. These exchanges were not recorded.

## Who Returned Worksheets

- **Version A:** 52 worksheets returned. Six pupils assigned this version were absent.
- **Version B:** 49 worksheets returned. Five pupils assigned this version were absent.

Only returned worksheets were analysed.

## How Answers Were Scored

A scorer who could not see the worksheet layout scored transcribed answers to the final explanation question. One point was awarded for stating that the amount of water was unchanged. One point was awarded for explaining that vessel shape changed the water level. A "fully credited" answer earned both points.

Ten transcribed answers were scored a second time by another scorer. The scorers agreed on nine. Discussion resolved the tenth before the final totals were compiled. This check helps describe the scoring procedure, but it is not a full reliability study.

## Results

| Score on the final question | Version A (52 worksheets) | Version B (49 worksheets) |
|---|---|---|
| Both points (fully credited) | 31 | 27 |
| One point | 15 | 16 |
| Zero points | 6 | 6 |

Fully credited answers made up a somewhat larger share of Version A worksheets than Version B worksheets. These scores come from one question. They do not measure pupils' general understanding of volume. No baseline task was scored, so the starting knowledge of the two groups is unknown.

## Limitations

- **Layout and class differences are mixed together.** Each version was used by two classes, so differences between classes could account for some or all of the result.
- **Teacher assistance was not recorded.** Teachers could answer questions during the lesson, and those exchanges are unknown.
- **Pupil assignment was not controlled.** Teachers chose the version for their classes, so the groups may differ in ways this comparison does not capture.
- **Absences and returns are excluded.** Eleven assigned pupils did not return worksheets, and the analysis does not include them.
- **Scoring reliability was checked only lightly.** Nine of ten double-scored answers matched, which is not enough for a full reliability estimate.
- **Preference was not measured.** No question asked which layout pupils preferred.

## What This Evaluation Shows and Does Not Show

This evaluation provides a concrete comparison of the returned answers. It shows that, in these classes, a somewhat larger share of answers earned full credit on the Version A layout. It does not show that the side-by-side layout was responsible for the difference.

A more controlled evaluation would need to record which version each pupil received, the classes and teachers involved, any teacher assistance during the lesson, absences and non-returns, and a baseline measure of starting knowledge. It would also need a fuller scoring reliability check and, if layout preference matters, a direct preference question.

## What we compared

Pupils completed a worksheet asking them to explain why the same amount of water looks different in a tall vessel and in a wide vessel. There were two versions:

- **Version A** placed a diagram beside each question.
- **Version B** placed the same diagrams together on a separate reference page.

Apart from diagram placement, the two versions were identical in wording, diagrams, and question order.

## How the materials were used

Four classes used the worksheets during one lesson. Two classes received Version A and two received Version B. Teachers chose the version for their classes before seeing any pupil responses.

All teachers used the same written instructions. They were free to answer questions during the lesson, and those exchanges were not recorded.

## Who was included

| | Version A | Version B |
|---|---|---|
| Returned worksheets (analysed) | 52 | 49 |
| Assigned but absent (not analysed) | 6 | 5 |

The analysis includes only returned worksheets.

## How answers were scored

A scorer assessed transcribed answers to the final explanation question without seeing which layout each pupil had used. Each answer could earn up to two points:

- 1 point for stating that the amount of water was unchanged
- 1 point for explaining that the vessel's shape changed the water level

To check consistency, a second scorer rescored ten transcribed answers. The two scorers agreed on nine. They resolved the tenth through discussion before the final totals were compiled. This check is enough to describe the procedure, but it is not a full reliability study.

| 1 point | 15 (about 29%) | 16 (about 33%) |
| 0 points | 6 (about 12%) | 6 (about 12%) |

In these classes, the side-by-side layout (Version A) was associated with a somewhat larger share of fully credited answers. These are scores on a single question. They are not a measure of pupils' general understanding of volume.

## What this comparison cannot tell us

- **Layout versus class differences.** Teachers assigned versions by class, not pupil by pupil. Differences between the classes could account for the gap.
- **Layout versus teacher help.** Teachers' answers to questions during the lesson were not recorded. Those exchanges may have affected responses differently in different classes.
- **Starting knowledge.** No earlier baseline task was scored, so we do not know whether the groups began with similar understanding.
- **Absent pupils.** Eleven assigned pupils (six for A, five for B) were absent and are not reflected in the results.
- **Pupil preference.** No preference question was asked, so the evaluation does not show which layout pupils preferred.

For these reasons, neither pupil assignment nor teacher assistance can be treated as controlled in this comparison.

The completed evaluation gives a concrete comparison of the returned answers from four classes. It also identifies what a more controlled evaluation would need to record: how pupils are assigned to versions, what help teachers give during the lesson, pupils' starting knowledge, and, if preference matters, pupils' views on each layout.

# Diagram Placement on a Volume Worksheet: A Comparison in Four Classes

## Summary

We compared two layouts of the same worksheet in four classes. In Version A, each question had its diagram beside it. In Version B, the same diagrams were grouped together on a separate reference page.

On the final explanation question, 31 of 52 returned Version A worksheets received full credit. For Version B, 27 of 49 did. The layout with a diagram beside each question was therefore associated with a somewhat larger share of fully credited answers.

This difference cannot be attributed to layout alone, for three reasons:

- Teachers chose which version their classes used.
- Teachers' help during the lesson was not recorded.
- Pupils' starting knowledge was not measured.

## What was compared

Both versions asked pupils to explain why the same amount of water looks different in a tall vessel and in a wide vessel. The wording, the diagrams and the order of questions were identical. The only difference was where the diagrams appeared:

- **Version A:** a diagram beside each question.
- **Version B:** all the same diagrams together on a reference page.

## How the materials were used

Four classes used the worksheets during one lesson. Two classes received Version A and two received Version B. Teachers chose the version for their classes before seeing any pupil responses. The evaluation therefore did not control which pupils received which version.

All teachers used the same written instructions. They were free to answer pupils' questions during the lesson, and those exchanges were not recorded.

Pupils returned 52 Version A worksheets and 49 Version B worksheets. Six further pupils assigned Version A and five assigned Version B were absent. The analysis includes only returned worksheets.

## How answers were scored

Answers to the final explanation question were transcribed. They were then scored by someone who could not see which layout each pupil had used. The scoring rule awarded:

- 1 point for stating that the amount of water was unchanged
- 1 point for explaining that the vessel's shape changed the water level

A second scorer re-scored ten of the transcribed answers. The two scorers agreed on nine. They resolved the tenth by discussion before the final totals were compiled. This small check is reported to describe the procedure. It is not a full study of how reliably the rule can be applied.

## Results

| Score on final question | Version A (diagram beside each question) | Version B (diagrams on reference page) |
|---|---|---|
| 2 points | 31 (60%) | 27 (55%) |
| 1 point | 15 (29%) | 16 (33%) |
| 0 points | 6 (12%) | 6 (12%) |
| **Returned worksheets** | **52** | **49** |

*Percentages are of returned worksheets, rounded to the nearest whole number, so a column may not total exactly 100%.*

Version A had a somewhat larger share of answers awarded both points. The number of answers scoring zero was the same in each group.

These are scores on a single question. They are not a measure of pupils' general understanding of volume.

## What the results cannot tell us

- **Layout versus class differences.** Each version was used by different classes, and teachers chose which version each class received. Differences between the classes could account for some or all of the gap.
- **Starting knowledge.** No earlier baseline task was scored, so we do not know whether the two groups began with similar understanding.
- **Teacher assistance.** Teachers could answer questions during the lesson, and these exchanges were not recorded. The amount or kind of help may have differed between classes.
- **Scoring reliability.** The second-scorer check covered only ten answers.
- **Pupil preference.** Pupils were not asked which layout they preferred, so the evaluation says nothing about preference.

## Conclusion

In these four classes, the worksheet with a diagram beside each question was associated with a somewhat larger share of fully credited answers on the final question. The evaluation cannot separate the effect of layout from class differences or from classroom assistance.

What the completed work provides is a concrete comparison of these returned answers. It also gives a record of what a more controlled evaluation would need to capture:

- how classes come to receive each version
- pupils' starting knowledge
- teacher–pupil exchanges during the lesson
- a fuller check of scoring reliability
- if preference is of interest, a question asking pupils about it

The waiting list has grown, and the proposed answer is to divide every returning gardener’s bed in half. I understand the appeal: there are twenty full beds and ten households waiting, and access to shared land should not depend on having joined years ago. But fairness involves more than the size of each plot. It also involves how we move from one allocation to another, including whether gardeners can keep established crops through their growing cycles. For that reason, I support dividing vacant beds first and allowing returning gardeners to keep their present beds for one more season.

Four full beds will become vacant at the end of this season. Dividing them would create eight half beds for the coming season. If every offer is accepted, eight households would receive beds and two would remain waiting. That is a real shortfall, not a cleared waiting list. The proposal would nevertheless open places for most households now waiting without requiring every returning gardener to remove established planting at once.

The strongest objection is that protecting established planting may also protect an established advantage. Sometimes it does. Planting a perennial cannot give someone a permanent claim to shared land, and our membership agreement promises a bed for one season, with renewal decided annually. The justification for this proposal is therefore a limited transition, not an entitlement to continued occupancy. Returning gardeners would keep their current beds for one more season, and the committee would publish the following season’s allocation rule before renewals open.

That advance notice must apply to new members as well. A household accepting a half bed needs to know the rules governing its future, just as a returning gardener does. If new members learn only afterward that their beds will be merged or moved, we will have reproduced the same uncertainty on smaller plots. The published rule should cover both groups. I do not yet have a preferred permanent bed size; we can decide how to manage this transition without claiming to have settled the permanent allocation.

The raised beds also require separate consideration. Two of the twenty full beds are reserved for gardeners who need them, and neither is among the four becoming vacant. My proposal preserves that reservation and the existing access assessment. Equal area does not necessarily mean equal access: a standard half bed is not automatically a substitute for a raised bed.

Location presents a further limitation. All four vacancies are at the far end of the site, so all eight new households would begin in the same area. Voluntary exchanges with returning members could help, but they cannot be counted as a guaranteed part of the proposal. Nor should a household have to negotiate a private favor to obtain a usable route to its bed. Before making offers, the committee should check the paths to the new half beds and report any access problem it cannot resolve.

Offers would follow the waiting list’s current order. This preserves whatever disadvantages households faced in learning about the list, and that concern deserves attention. But changing the order during this allocation would introduce another contested decision without advance notice to those affected. We should begin reviewing how the list is advertised now and announce any future change in ordering before it applies.

The choice before the meeting is therefore between transitions with different costs. Dividing vacant beds first would leave two households waiting if all eight offers are accepted. Dividing occupied beds immediately might create more places, while spreading disruption across more gardeners and established crops. I support the vacancy-first transition because it expands access substantially while limiting immediate disruption and requiring advance notice of the next allocation rule. That judgment does not erase the cost to those still waiting. The meeting should weigh that cost alongside the disruption of immediate division, with neither left out of the decision.

**Position Statement: Dividing Vacant Beds Before Occupied Ones**

The waiting list has grown, and one proposed answer is to divide every returning gardener's bed in half. I understand why that seems like a fair place to begin. There are twenty full beds and ten households waiting, and nobody wants membership to depend on having joined years ago. But land is not the only thing we are allocating. We are also allocating the chance to carry a crop through its growing cycle. For that reason, I propose that we divide vacant beds this season and leave occupied beds intact for one more season, while the committee settles a published rule for the seasons that follow.

**What the proposal would and would not do**

Four full beds will become vacant at the end of this season. Dividing them would create eight half beds. If every offer is accepted, that leaves two households on the current waiting list without a bed. That shortfall is real, and I do not want to obscure it: this proposal would not clear the waiting list, and we should not describe eight offers as though it does. What it would do is let us make a substantial number of offers, eight out of ten, without requiring every returning gardener to remove established planting at once. The rest of this statement explains why I think that trade is worth making and what safeguards it needs.

**A transition, not an entitlement**

Some members have suggested that "established planting" is simply another name for established advantage. Sometimes it may be, and I do not think a person who has planted a perennial has acquired a permanent claim to shared land. Nor could I argue that they have: the membership agreement promises a bed for a season, with renewal decided annually. My case is narrower. Disruption to crops already in the ground is a real cost, and a one-season transition lets us avoid imposing it on everyone at once while we decide the longer-term rule properly. Under this proposal, returning gardeners would keep their present beds for one more season, and the committee would publish the following season's allocation rule before renewals open. No returning gardener would come away with a stronger claim than the agreement already gives them.

**Certainty for new members too**

That published rule matters as much for new members as for returning ones. If a household accepts a half bed now and learns afterward that half beds will be merged or moved next year, we will have recreated the same uncertainty on a smaller piece of ground. The rule should therefore cover current and new members alike. I do not yet have a preferred permanent bed size, and I am not asking the meeting to choose one tonight. The transition can be decided without pretending the permanent question is already settled; in fact, separating the two is what gives us time to settle the second one fairly.

**Safeguards**

Three conditions should accompany the proposal.

*Raised beds stay outside the arithmetic.* Two of the twenty full beds are raised beds reserved for gardeners who need them, and neither is among the four becoming vacant. My proposal keeps that reservation and leaves the existing access assessment unchanged. A standard half bed is not automatically a substitute for a raised bed, even if the plan counts its area the same way.

We could invite returning members to exchange locations voluntarily, but I do not want to count such exchanges as a guaranteed part of the proposal, and no new household should have to negotiate a private favor to get a usable route to its bed. The committee should check the paths to the new half beds before making offers and report to members any access problem it cannot resolve.

*The waiting list keeps its current order for these offers.* I recognise that preserving the order also preserves whatever disadvantages people faced in learning about the list. Changing it now, however, would add another contested decision to this allocation without giving households notice. A review of how the list is advertised can begin immediately, and any future change to the ordering should be announced before it takes effect.

I would like the next set of fraction worksheets to include one worked example followed by a problem that asks pupils to explain a different method. Our current sheets give a sequence of steps and then ask pupils to repeat it. This is useful when the immediate aim is to practise the sequence. I propose revising the report template to make exclusions visible without changing which runs contribute to the reported mean. The summary would show the mean alongside the number of runs attempted and the number retained. A separate table, labeled “Record of exclusions,” would account for the difference by listing each excluded run’s identifier, completion status, reason for exclusion, and whether a usable reading exists. Raw readings would remain in the underlying record, available through the existing review process.

The current summary lists only the runs used to calculate the mean. This makes the mean easy to read, but it prevents readers from distinguishing a batch with no exclusions from one whose exclusions have simply disappeared from view. The proposed table would make those decisions inspectable. It would not require excluded readings to enter the mean or alter the existing exclusion rule.

Two examples illustrate why that distinction matters. A run stopped because the temperature controller failed did not meet the stated measurement conditions. A completed run with an unusual result has not, for that reason alone, failed those conditions. Our existing rule therefore excludes controller failures and retains unusual completed results unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies exclusion. The table would show how that rule was applied.

The table must also include excluded runs that produced no usable reading. Listing only excluded numeric values would conceal those failures and could make a difficult batch appear cleaner than it was. At the same time, stopped runs should not be treated as measured outcomes. Reporting attempted and retained counts beside the mean would preserve that distinction while allowing readers to account for every run.

Greater visibility carries a risk: readers may try to calculate a new mean from everything reported. Clearly labeling the table and recording every exclusion reason may reduce that risk, but cannot eliminate it. # Revised Proposal: Reporting Excluded Runs in the Batch Summary

## Summary

I propose that the report template include a separate **exclusions table** that records every run removed from the reported mean, along with the reason for each exclusion. The summary would also state how many runs were attempted and how many were retained. This change makes the existing exclusion decisions visible. It does not change which runs are excluded, and it does not propose that every excluded reading enter the mean.

## Current Problem

The final summary lists only the runs used to calculate the reported mean. That presentation is convenient, but it leaves a reader unable to tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether exclusions were removed from view. A batch with three stopped runs and a batch with none can produce identical summaries.

## Two Kinds of Exclusion

The proposal depends on distinguishing two cases that the current rule already treats differently.

1. **Controller failure (run stopped).** The run was stopped because the temperature controller failed. The stated measurement conditions were not met, so the run is excluded.
2. **Completed run with an unusual result.** The run finished, but its result looks unusual. An unusual result alone does not show that the conditions failed. Under the existing rule, the run is **retained** unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies exclusion.

The exclusions table would expose how this rule was applied to each run. It would not change the rule.

## Proposed Table Contents

Each excluded run would appear as one row with four fields:

- **Run identifier**
- **Completion status** (for example, stopped or completed)
- **Reason** for exclusion, stated as documented
- **Usable reading exists** (yes or no)

Raw readings would not be added to this table. They would remain in the underlying record and stay available through the existing review process. Keeping the table to decisions makes the exclusions easier to scan.

## Runs With No Usable Reading

A table listing only excluded numeric values would omit runs that produced nothing usable. That omission could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was. The summary therefore reports:

- the **number attempted**,
- the **number retained** beside the mean,

and the exclusions table accounts for the difference. Stopped runs are not counted as measured outcomes, which would distort the mean in the other direction.

## Shared Explanations for Grouped Faults

When one fault affects several runs, a shared explanation for that group may be used to reduce repeated prose. Each affected run must still appear as its own row, so the batch's history remains countable.

## Limits and Open Tradeoffs

This proposal does not solve every problem, and the following tradeoffs remain open:

- **Documented reasons may be weak or inaccurate.** A fuller table cannot guarantee honest recording, and reviewers will still need to judge whether each stated reason is convincing.
- **The existing rule may be ambiguous.** The rule for retaining unusual completed results depends on a separately recorded fault. If that record is missing, the table cannot repair the ambiguity.
- **Readers may recalculate.** Showing failed runs may encourage readers to compute a new mean from everything visible. The table is labeled as a record of exclusions to discourage this, but the label may not prevent it.
- **Reporting takes time.** Recording each affected run adds work, especially when one fault affects many runs.

Decide whether the four-field format is sufficient, whether grouped explanations should be permitted, and how reviewers will judge documented reasons. The policy has not been adopted, and the existing exclusion rule remains unchanged.

- *Reporting time.* The extra reporting takes time, especially when one fault affects several runs. We could permit a shared explanation for such a group, provided each affected run still appears in the table. That reduces repeated prose and keeps the batch's history countable. Whether this saves enough time to justify the added reporting is not settled.

**Proposal: report excluded runs in a separate table**

I propose that the report template include a separate table of excluded runs, with the reason for each exclusion. The final summary now lists only the runs used to calculate the reported mean. A reader of that summary cannot tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether the exclusions were dropped from the summary. The proposal does not change which readings enter the mean.

**The existing rule stays as it is.** A run stopped because the temperature controller failed did not meet the stated measurement conditions. A completed run with an unusual result has not shown that the conditions failed. Our rule excludes controller failures and keeps unusual completed results, unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies excluding them. The table would show how that rule was applied.

**Proposed contents.** For each excluded run, the table would give the run identifier, completion status, reason, and whether a usable reading exists. Raw readings would stay in the underlying record, available through the existing review process. Adding them to the table is unnecessary for showing the decisions and would make those decisions harder to see. Runs with no usable reading must appear too. A table of excluded numeric values alone would miss them and could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was.

**Counts in the summary.** Stopped runs should not be counted as measured outcomes, since that would distort the results in the other direction. The summary should instead report the number attempted and the number retained beside the mean, and the exclusions table would account for the difference.

**Open tradeoffs.**

- *Readers recomputing the mean.* Showing excluded runs may lead readers to compute a new mean from everything listed. That may happen. We would label the table as a record of exclusions and give every reason, even where it repeats an earlier one.
- *Reviewer judgment.* Reviewers will still have to decide whether the documented reasons are convincing. A fuller table cannot guarantee honest recording or fix an ambiguous rule. It makes the decisions available for inspection.
- *Reporting effort.* The extra reporting takes time, especially when one fault affects several runs. We could allow a single shared explanation for such a group, with each affected run still listed. This cuts repeated prose and keeps the batch's history countable. Whether it saves enough effort to justify the added table is the question for the meeting.

**Claim.** Let \((a_n)_{n\ge1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing real sequence with limit zero, and put
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then each \(d_n\ge0\), and
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1.
\]
For every integer \(N\ge1\), the tail after \(N\) terms is
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, this tail is less than any prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) when \(N\) is sufficiently large.

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\ge a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\ge0\).

To find the sum of the series, first consider its partial sum:
\[
S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1}).
\]
Every intermediate term cancels, leaving
\[
S_N=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\]
Thus
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Because \(a_{N+1}\) tends to zero, the partial sums \(S_N\) approach \(a_1\). By definition, this means that the series converges to \(a_1\).

Now fix \(N\ge1\). For any integer \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})
=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\]
The difference between this finite tail sum and \(a_{N+1}\) has absolute value \(a_{M+1}\), which tends to zero as \(M\) increases. Hence the infinite tail converges and equals
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]

Finally, let \(\varepsilon>0\). Since \(a_n\to0\), there is an integer \(K\ge1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) for every \(k\ge K\). For every \(N\ge K\), we therefore have
\[
0\le\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]

No strict decrease is needed: equal consecutive terms simply give \(d_n=0\). If \(a_1=0\), nonnegativity and monotonicity force every \(a_n=0\), and all the identities still hold. \(\square\)

**Theorem.** Let (a_n), n ≥ 1, be a sequence of real numbers that is nonnegative (a_n ≥ 0 for all n), nonincreasing (a_(n+1) ≤ a_n for all n), and has limit zero. Define d_n = a_n − a_(n+1). Then:

1. d_n ≥ 0 for every n.
2. The series d_1 + d_2 + d_3 + ... converges, and its sum is a_1.
3. For every integer N ≥ 1, the tail d_(N+1) + d_(N+2) + ... converges, and its sum is exactly a_(N+1).
4. For every ε > 0 there is an N such that the tail after N terms is less than ε.

**Before the proof: what "converges" means here.** A series converges when its partial sums approach a limit. The partial sum S_N is the sum of the first N terms. To say S_N → L means: for every ε > 0, there is an index beyond which every S_N lies within ε of L. We will verify this directly from the definition, using only the hypothesis a_n → 0. No convergence test or other theorem about series is needed.

**Proof.**

*Step 1: the terms are nonnegative.* Because the sequence is nonincreasing, a_(n+1) ≤ a_n, so d_n = a_n − a_(n+1) ≥ 0. (If two consecutive terms are equal, then d_n = 0. That is allowed. Nothing below requires d_n to be strictly positive.)

*Step 2: the partial sums telescope.* Fix N ≥ 1 and add up the first N terms:

```
S_N = d_1 + d_2 + ... + d_N
    = (a_1 − a_2) + (a_2 − a_3) + ... + (a_N − a_(N+1)).
```

Every term except the very first a_1 and the very last a_(N+1) appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign. Those pairs cancel, leaving

```
S_N = a_1 − a_(N+1).        (A)
```

This is an exact identity for every N. It is the whole engine of the proof.

*Step 3: the series converges to a_1.* By (A), the distance from S_N to a_1 is

```
|S_N − a_1| = |−a_(N+1)| = a_(N+1),
```

using a_(N+1) ≥ 0. Now use the hypothesis a_n → 0 in its definition form: for a given ε > 0, there is an index K such that a_k < ε whenever k ≥ K. If N ≥ K, then N + 1 ≥ K as well, so

```
|S_N − a_1| = a_(N+1) < ε.
```

This is exactly the statement that S_N → a_1. So the series converges and its sum is a_1. This proves item 2.

*Step 4: the tail also telescopes.* Fix N ≥ 1. The tail after N terms is itself a series, d_(N+1) + d_(N+2) + ..., and its partial sums are the finite sums from n = N + 1 up to some M > N. Call that finite sum T_(N,M). It telescopes in the same way:

```
T_(N,M) = (a_(N+1) − a_(N+2)) + (a_(N+2) − a_(N+3)) + ... + (a_M − a_(M+1))
        = a_(N+1) − a_(M+1).        (B)
```

*Step 5: the tail converges to a_(N+1).* Keep N fixed and let M grow. By (B),

```
|T_(N,M) − a_(N+1)| = a_(M+1).
```

Given ε > 0, take the same K as in Step 3. If M ≥ K, then a_(M+1) < ε, so T_(N,M) is within ε of a_(N+1). Hence the tail partial sums converge to a_(N+1). That is, the tail after N terms has the exact value a_(N+1). This proves item 3.

*Step 6: the tail can be made small.* Given ε > 0, choose K as above and set N = max(1, K). Then N + 1 ≥ K, so the tail after N terms equals a_(N+1) < ε. This proves item 4.

**Remarks on edge cases.**

- If a_1 = 0, then every a_n satisfies 0 ≤ a_n ≤ a_1 = 0, so the sequence is identically zero. Every d_n is zero, identities (A) and (B) still hold, and the theorem says that the zero series sums to zero. No separate argument is needed.
- The proof never divided by anything, never assumed the a_n were strictly decreasing, and never assumed the d_n were positive. It used only three facts: a_n ≥ 0, a_(n+1) ≤ a_n, and a_n → 0.

**Why the result is useful.** The theorem turns a question about an infinite sum into a question about a single term of the original sequence. The partial sum S_N misses the true total by exactly a_(N+1). So if you want the sum accurate to within ε, you need only find an index where the original sequence has dropped below ε. ∎

**Theorem.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence of real numbers with $a_n \ge 0$, $a_{n+1}\le a_n$ for every $n$, and $a_n \to 0$. Define
$$
d_n = a_n - a_{n+1}, \qquad n \ge 1.
$$
Then every $d_n$ is nonnegative, the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges with
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n = a_1,
$$
and for every integer $N \ge 1$ the tail of the series after $N$ terms equals $a_{N+1}$. In particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

**Proof.**

*Step 1: the terms are nonnegative.* Since the sequence is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1} \le a_n$, so
$$
d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0 \qquad \text{for every } n \ge 1.
$$

*Step 2: the partial sums telescope.* Fix an integer $N \ge 1$ and write out the $N$-th partial sum. Each $a_k$ with $2 \le k \le N$ appears once with a plus sign (from $d_k$) and once with a minus sign (from $d_{k-1}$), so all of these cancel:
$$
\begin{aligned}
S_N := \sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n
&= (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + \cdots + (a_N - a_{N+1}) \\
&= a_1 - a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The same cancellation applies to any block of consecutive terms. For integers $M > N \ge 1$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{N,M} := \sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n
&= (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + (a_{N+2} - a_{N+3}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1}) \\
&= a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Both identities are exact for every finite $N$ and $M$; no limit has been taken yet.

*Step 3: the series converges to $a_1$.* By definition, $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges to $a_1$ if the partial sums $S_N$ approach $a_1$, that is, if $|S_N - a_1|$ can be made as small as we like by taking $N$ large. From Step 2,
$$
|S_N - a_1| = |-a_{N+1}| = a_{N+1},
$$
where the absolute value disappears because $a_{N+1} \ge 0$. Now use the hypothesis $a_n \to 0$ directly. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, there is an integer $K$ such that
$$
a_k < \varepsilon \qquad \text{whenever } k \ge K .
$$
If $N \ge K$, then $N + 1 \ge K$, so
$$
|S_N - a_1| = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon .
$$
This is exactly the statement that $S_N \to a_1$. Hence the series converges and its sum is $a_1$.

*Step 4: the tail after $N$ terms equals $a_{N+1}$.* Fix $N \ge 1$. The tail after $N$ terms is $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n$, the limit of the finite sums $T_{N,M}$ as $M \to \infty$. From Step 2,
$$
T_{N,M} = a_{N+1} - a_{M+1},
$$
and $a_{M+1} \to 0$ as $M \to \infty$ by hypothesis, while $a_{N+1}$ does not depend on $M$. Therefore
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = \lim_{M\to\infty} \left( a_{N+1} - a_{M+1} \right) = a_{N+1}.
$$
This agrees with computing the tail as the full sum minus the $N$-th partial sum:
$$
a_1 - S_N = a_1 - (a_1 - a_{N+1}) = a_{N+1}.
$$

*Step 5: the tail can be made smaller than any $\varepsilon$.* Given $\varepsilon > 0$, take $K$ as in Step 3, so that $a_k < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$, and set $N = \max(1, K)$. Then $N + 1 \ge K$, and by Step 4
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon .
$$

*Two remarks on edge cases.* If $a_1 = 0$, then $0 \le a_n \le a_1 = 0$ forces every $a_n$ to be zero, every $d_n$ to be zero, and the identities above all read $0 = 0$. If two consecutive terms are equal, say $a_n = a_{n+1}$, then $d_n = 0$; nothing in the argument required strict decrease, only $a_{n+1} \le a_n$. $\blacksquare$

In particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

The whole argument rests on the fact that consecutive terms of $d_n$ cancel when added. Fix an integer $N \ge 1$ and write out the partial sum $S_N = \sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n$ term by term:

$$
