A scoring guide can increase agreement among teachers without improving the validity of their judgments: raters may agree yet remain jointly mistaken about what a response demonstrates. We revised the guide after an initial review revealed disagreements about whether an explanation constituted reasoning or merely repeated the question. The revision introduced paired examples illustrating this boundary. It did not add questions, change the maximum score of 20, or change the intended construct. Whether the revised guide preserved that construct in practice, however, remains an empirical question.

Eight teachers scored 48 short responses in two rounds, with each response rated by the same two teachers in both rounds and each teacher scoring 12 responses per round. Teachers used the original guide in the first round and, following a workshop, the revised guide in the second. The rounds were separated by one week. Response order changed between rounds, and teachers could not view their earlier scores. These procedures reduced opportunities for direct copying but did not rule out memory of individual responses.

The number of responses for which the two ratings differed by more than two points decreased from 16 of 48 to 7 of 48. The mean of all 96 ratings, reported to one decimal place, increased from 12.4 to 12.8. Because pupils did not produce new responses between rounds, this increase represents a change in scoring rather than improved pupil performance. No external criterion was available to determine whether either round’s mean was closer to an appropriate value.

The decrease in disagreements exceeding two points suggests that the revised guide and workshop together may help teachers apply a shared boundary between reasoning and repetition. Their separate contributions cannot be determined because both were introduced between rounds. Moreover, the use of repeated responses limits conclusions about scoring unfamiliar work. These limitations do not negate the observed decrease in disagreement, but they constrain its interpretation. Further study would require fresh responses and an independent account of response quality. The observed result is greater agreement on the specified measure; consistency on new work remains an open question, and validity has not been established by making ratings more alike.

We evaluated a denoising setting for spoken archive clips using three separate assessments: listener preference, a transcript audit, and processing time. A cleaner background was useful only if the words were preserved, so listener preference alone was not sufficient evidence of success. Timing was assessed because the archive team wants to audition settings interactively, but the measurement did not represent a full editing session.

In the preference study, 12 listeners each heard both versions of 30 clips and selected the denoised version, the original, or no preference. Version order was counterbalanced within the listening protocol. The study yielded 360 choices, not 360 independent listeners or clips. Of these choices, 214 favored the denoised version, 118 favored the original, and 28 indicated no preference. For the 18 noisy clips, the corresponding counts were 152, 50, and 14. For the 12 quieter clips, they were 62, 68, and 14. The aggregate counts therefore obscure a different preference balance for quieter material, where the original received slightly more choices than the denoised version.

The separate transcript audit found at least one word transcribed differently between versions in three of the 30 clips, all in the noisy subset. This result counts clips with a difference, not the total number of changed words. A second auditor confirmed that the transcript pairs differed but did not establish which version better represented the recording. The differences therefore cannot all be classified as errors introduced by denoising. Likewise, preference for a denoised clip does not establish that its words were preserved.

In a separate timing run on the same workstation, processing 200 fixed audio frames took a median of 42 milliseconds per frame with the existing setting and 71 milliseconds with the new setting. These measurements cover processing of the tested frames and exclude input loading. They do not measure the interface delay experienced by editors.

The findings support offering the new setting for audition on noisy material while retaining access to the original. They do not justify automatically replacing every clip. The transcript differences remain unresolved and require review before the setting is used for a final archive render.

# Revised Discussion: Recording Trial

The recording trial was prompted by a backlog, and speed was the immediate reason for trying the new form. The concern we kept in view, however, was that a faster route could produce a record that could not be interpreted later. The photo-led form requires a scaled overview and four mandatory fields. The drawing-led form uses the same four fields plus a hand-drawn plan. Both allow free-text notes on relationships with adjacent deposits. These optional notes sit outside the completeness check, which limits what the check can tell us.

We used the drawing-led form for the first 18 contexts recorded in a trench and the photo-led form for the next 18. The later contexts were generally shallower. The same two recorders worked throughout and could ask each other for help, but we did not record who supplied that help. The trial is therefore a shared-work comparison of consecutive context groups, not a balanced comparison of independent individual performance.

Two of the 18 photo-led records and six of the 18 drawing-led records omitted at least one mandatory field on first submission. Median recording times were 11 minutes for the photo-led form and 16 minutes for the drawing-led form. These times cover the initial record and exclude later corrections. Seven photo-led records and 13 drawing-led records included an optional relationship note. A lower count of such notes could mean that fewer relationships were visible, that the form elicited less description, or both. No independent inventory of relationships existed against which the notes could be checked, so we cannot separate these explanations.

The evidence therefore points in two directions. By the mandatory-field measure, the photo-led records were more complete. They also contained fewer of the optional notes that might matter for later interpretation. Each reading has a flaw. Calling the photo-led records simply more complete lets the measure stand in for the record itself. Calling them poorer because they contain fewer notes assumes that the missing notes represent lost information, which we cannot confirm. The backlog made this distinction easy to lose: saving five minutes was immediately useful, while any interpretive information left out would become costly only later.

We propose continuing the photo-led form on a limited set of contexts, adding an explicit relationship prompt, and tracking correction time. This proposal is not an evaluated improvement. The trial shows an association between the photo-led form and faster initial recording and fewer mandatory omissions in these consecutive groups. It does not isolate a form effect, and it does not show that the resulting archive retains every relationship needed for interpretation. The explicit relationship prompt is intended to make that retention testable, so that the next stage can examine whether the photo-led form loses information that the drawing-led form captured.
